name: Hammer toe
aliases: PIP flexion deformity of the lesser toe

reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: A hammer toe is a flexion deformity at the proximal interphalangeal joint, often with compensatory extension at the metatarsophalangeal joint and a neutral or extended distal interphalangeal joint
This is the key contrast with claw toe (metatarsophalangeal hyperextension plus flexion at both interphalangeal joints) and mallet toe (isolated distal interphalangeal flexion)
The second toe is most commonly affected, and the deformity frequently accompanies hallux valgus that crowds the lesser toes
A dorsal corn over the prominent proximal interphalangeal joint and an end-of-toe callosity are typical pressure lesions
Determining whether the deformity is flexible or fixed is essential, as passively correctable deformities are amenable to soft-tissue procedures while rigid ones require bony correction
Standing examination and weight-bearing radiographs help define associated metatarsophalangeal subluxation and forefoot alignment
Conservative care includes roomy, deep toe-box footwear, silicone toe sleeves or splints, corn padding, and toe-crest orthoses
Surgical options range from flexor-to-extensor tendon transfer and extensor lengthening for flexible deformity to proximal interphalangeal joint arthrodesis or resection for fixed deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Hammer toe arises from an imbalance between the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the lesser toe that leaves the proximal interphalangeal joint flexed. When the intrinsic muscles fail to stabilise the metatarsophalangeal joint, the long extensor hyperextends that joint while the long flexor and the geometry of the toe pull the proximal interphalangeal joint into flexion. Ill-fitting, tight, or high-heeled footwear that crowds the toes is a major extrinsic contributor, and adjacent hallux valgus commonly displaces and deforms the second toe. Initially the deformity is flexible and passively correctable, but with time capsular and tendon contractures make it rigid. The elevated proximal interphalangeal joint rubs against the shoe to form a painful dorsal corn, and abnormal loading produces callosities at the tip of the toe and beneath the metatarsal head.
additionalDifferentials: Claw toe with metatarsophalangeal hyperextension and combined interphalangeal flexion
Mallet toe with isolated distal interphalangeal flexion
Crossover second toe from plantar plate insufficiency
Rheumatoid or other inflammatory forefoot deformity
Freiberg's infraction of a lesser metatarsal head
additionalInvestigations: Standing clinical examination to define the deformed joints and test flexibility with the push-up or Kelikian test
Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and lateral foot radiographs to assess metatarsophalangeal alignment and subluxation
Assessment for associated hallux valgus and forefoot deformity
Neurological examination to detect an underlying neuromuscular cause when deformities are multiple
Vascular assessment of the toe before considering surgery
Inflammatory markers and relevant serology if inflammatory arthritis is suspected
Pedobarography where transfer metatarsalgia accompanies the deformity
redFlags: Multiple or symmetrical lesser-toe deformities suggesting an underlying neuromuscular disorder or inflammatory arthritis
Ulceration or infection of a corn or the toe tip, particularly in diabetes or peripheral vascular disease
Signs of digital ischaemia or poor perfusion that jeopardise healing
Rapidly progressive deformity with pain and swelling indicating inflammatory or neuropathic pathology
reference.prognosis: Flexible hammer toes are often well controlled with footwear and orthotic measures, and soft-tissue surgery corrects them reliably. Fixed deformities respond well to arthrodesis or joint resection with good pain relief, although some residual stiffness, floating toe, recurrence, or malalignment can occur. Outcomes are poorer when an underlying neuromuscular disorder or inflammatory arthritis is not addressed.
pitfalls: Failing to test whether the deformity is flexible or fixed, leading to the wrong choice of procedure
Overlooking associated hallux valgus that crowds and deforms the second toe and will cause recurrence if untreated
Missing an underlying neuromuscular cause when several toes are involved
Neglecting foot perfusion and the diabetic status before operating on the toe
Ignoring metatarsophalangeal joint subluxation, so that isolated toe surgery leaves the deformity uncorrected
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
